The portfolio includes some of the most valuable luxury brands in the world: Louis Vuitton, Christian Dior, Tiffany & Co., Bulgari, Hennessy, Moët & Chandon, Dom Pérignon, TAG Heuer, and Sephora. Arnault built this luxury empire through a decades-long series of acquisitions, beginning with his purchase of the Boussac textile group (which included Christian Dior) in 1984 and continuing through the transformative 2021 acquisition of Tiffany & Co. for $15.8 billion, the largest luxury industry transaction in history. This acquisition-driven approach to value creation remains central to the family’s investment philosophy. Beyond LVMH, Arnault has made personal investments in technology and media. He has held a significant personal stake in Netflix and has invested in French media assets. The family’s investment activities through Agache and Groupe Arnault extend to real estate, including commercial properties in Paris and art-related investments. Arnault is one of the most significant private art collectors in the world, and the Louis Vuitton Foundation building in Paris, designed by Frank Gehry, houses part of the family’s art collection.
private_markets_approach: The Arnault family’s private markets activity is distinguished by its focus on luxury brand acquisition and development. LVMH’s corporate development team, working closely with the family, continuously evaluates potential brand acquisitions that could join the group’s portfolio. This approach treats brand building and acquisition as a form ofprivate equityinvesting, with LVMH providing management expertise, distribution infrastructure, and capital to accelerate growth of acquired brands. Outside LVMH, the family has made direct investments in technology startups and growth-stage companies, particularly in the French and European technology ecosystem. Bernard Arnault’s sons have been active in expanding the family’s technology investment footprint, with investments in e-commerce, digital luxury experiences, and consumer technology. The family’s real estate portfolio includes significant commercial properties in Paris, one of the world’s most valuable real estate markets. LVMH’s own real estate footprint, spanning flagship stores on major luxury shopping avenues globally, adds an additional dimension of real estate exposure within the operating company. Fund managers approaching the Arnault family should understand that investment decisions are heavily centralized around Bernard Arnault and a small circle of family members and advisors. The family’s investment thesis revolves around excellence, brand quality, and long-term value creation. Strategies connected to luxury, consumer premium, retail innovation, or European technology are most likely to align with the family’s interests.

description: Excession LLC is the family office of Elon Musk, managing the personal wealth of the world's wealthiest individual across holdings in Tesla, SpaceX, X…
investment_strategy: Musk’s investment strategy is fundamentally different from nearly every other family office at comparable scale. Rather than diversifying across asset classes and external managers, the vast majority of Musk’s wealth is concentrated in equity stakes in his own operating companies. His approximately 13% stake in Tesla represents the largest single component of his net worth, followed by an estimated 42% stake in SpaceX, which was valued at approximately $180 billion in its most recent secondary transactions. This concentration is a deliberate choice rather than a structural constraint. Musk has consistently channeled personal capital into his ventures, including a reported $44 billion acquisition of Twitter in 2022 (now X Corp), personal investment in xAI, and ongoing capital commitments to The Boring Company and Neuralink. The family office’s function is less aboutportfolio constructionand more about managing the financial complexity of holding controlling or significant stakes in multiple private and public companies simultaneously. Jared Birchall, who has served as Musk’s financial manager and head of Excession, oversees the day-to-day management of Musk’s financial affairs, including trust structures, liquidity management, and the coordination required across Musk’s various corporate interests.
private_markets_approach: Musk’s private markets exposure is almost entirely through his own companies. SpaceX, valued among the most valuable private companies globally, represents the single largest private holding. The company has raised capital through periodic primary rounds and has facilitated secondary sales for employees and early investors, but Musk has maintained a large ownership position throughout. xAI, founded in 2023, represents Musk’s newest major private company investment. The artificial intelligence venture raised significant capital in 2024, with Musk contributing personal funds alongside external investors. The Boring Company and Neuralink are earlier-stage private companies where Musk holds substantial equity positions. Fund managers should understand that Musk’s family office does not operate a traditional LP allocation program. The office does not broadly commit to externalventure capital,private equity, or real estate funds. Capital deployment decisions are driven by Musk’s own entrepreneurial ventures rather than portfolio diversification objectives. Any engagement with the family office would likely need to connect directly to the strategic interests of one of Musk’s operating companies.

Individual family members also maintain separate investment vehicles. Alice Walton has focused her efforts on art and philanthropy through Crystal Bridges Museum and the Alice L. Walton Foundation. These separate activities complement the centralized investment activities managed through Walton Enterprises. The family’s investment approach is conservative relative to its scale. Capital preservation and intergenerational wealth transfer are primary objectives, and the portfolio reflects a lower risk tolerance than many technology-oriented family offices of comparable size.
private_markets_approach: Walton Enterprises’ private markets activity centers on real estate, direct operating businesses, and selective venture andgrowth equityinvestments. The family has been a transformative force in northwest Arkansas real estate, investing billions in residential, commercial, and infrastructure development that has reshaped the region. In private equity, the family participates primarily through fund commitments to established managers, though direct co-investments occur selectively in industries where the family has operational expertise or strategic interest. Agriculture, supply chain technology, and sustainability are areas of particular focus, reflecting both the family’s retail heritage and its philanthropic priorities around environmental stewardship. Venture capital exposure has grown in recent years, with investments in agriculture technology, fintech, and logistics startups. The family’s deep understanding of retail supply chains and consumer behavior provides a differentiated lens for evaluating companies operating in adjacent spaces. Walton Enterprises also manages complex estate planning and intergenerational wealth transfer structures, including a network of trusts and holding entities designed to preserve family wealth across generations while maintaining governance alignment among family branches.

Mukesh Ambani has directed Reliance through a series of transformative investments that have reshaped entire sectors of the Indian economy. The most consequential of these was the launch of Jio Platforms in 2016, which disrupted India’s telecommunications industry by offering free voice calls and extremely low-cost mobile data. Jio invested over $35 billion in building a nationwide 4G network from scratch, acquired over 450 million subscribers within five years, and attracted over $20 billion in investment from global partners including Meta, Google, KKR, Silver Lake, and Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala. Reliance Retail, the family’s second major growth platform, has become India’s largest retailer with over 18,000 stores across grocery, electronics, fashion, and pharmacy categories. The retail business has attracted investment from global partners and is positioning for a potential public listing. The family’s third strategic pillar is green energy. Reliance has committed over $10 billion to building an integrated new energy business spanning solar panel manufacturing, battery storage, green hydrogen, and fuel cell technology. This investment reflects Ambani’s stated goal of transitioning Reliance from a fossil fuel company to a renewable energy leader by 2035. The Ambani family’s personal wealth management is conducted privately, with limited public disclosure beyond the Reliance shareholding. Real estate holdings include Antilia, the family’s 27-story private residence in Mumbai, which is among the most expensive residential properties in the world.
private_markets_approach: The Ambani family’s private markets activity operates primarily through Reliance Industries’ corporate development and venture functions rather than through an independent family office. The strategy mirrors the platform-building approach of Chinese technology conglomerates, creating a comprehensive digital services stack for Indian consumers and enterprises. In media and entertainment, Reliance acquired Network18, one of India’s largest media conglomerates, and merged its media assets with Disney’s Indian operations (Star India and Hotstar) in a deal valued at approximately $8.5 billion, creating India’s largest entertainment company. The Ambani family also invests in sports through ownership of the Mumbai Indians cricket franchise in the Indian Premier League and interests in football and other sporting ventures. These investments combine brand building with financial returns in India’s rapidly growing sports and entertainment market. Philanthropically, the family operates through the Reliance Foundation, led by Nita Ambani, which focuses on education, healthcare, rural transformation, and disaster response. The foundation operates one of the largest corporate social responsibility programs in India, with annual expenditures exceeding $100 million.

description: The Dumas family, controlling shareholders of Hermes International, manages approximately $100 billion in wealth derived from their majority stake in one…
investment_strategy: The Dumas family’s investment strategy is defined by its extraordinary concentration in a single asset: Hermes International. Unlike many ultra-wealthy families who diversify aggressively, the Dumas family has maintained its commitment to Hermes ownership as the primary vehicle for wealth creation and preservation. This conviction has been rewarded: Hermes shares have been among the best-performing luxury stocks globally, driven by the company’s pricing power, brand exclusivity, and disciplined growth strategy. The family’s governance structure, centered on H51, was designed specifically to prevent hostile acquisition and maintain family control. This structure became critical in 2010 when LVMH, led by Bernard Arnault, disclosed a 17% stake in Hermes built through equity derivatives. The family responded by consolidating their holdings and creating H51 as a defensive mechanism. LVMH ultimately distributed its Hermes shares to its own shareholders in 2014. Individual family members maintain personal investment portfolios that provide some diversification beyond the Hermes stake. These portfolios include French and European real estate, fixed income, and selective public equity positions. However, the scale of these personal investments is modest relative to the family’s Hermes holdings. The family’s approach to the Hermes business itself reflects an investment philosophy of quality over growth. Hermes has consistently resisted the aggressive retail expansion, licensing, and brand extension strategies pursued by competitors. This discipline has preserved brand exclusivity and pricing power, which in turn supports the long-term appreciation of family wealth.
private_markets_approach: The Dumas family’s private markets activity is limited relative to the family’s overall wealth, reflecting the conscious decision to keep capital concentrated in Hermes. Real estate is the most significant non-Hermes private markets exposure, with family members holding properties in Paris, the French countryside, and other European locations. Some family members have pursued personal investment interests, including art collecting and cultural philanthropy. The Fondation d’entreprise Hermes supports artisanal craftsmanship, contemporary art, and environmental sustainability, blending the family’s business heritage with philanthropic objectives. Hermes itself makes selective private investments through its operations, including acquisitions of tanneries, fabric manufacturers, and specialized workshops that secure the company’s supply chain. These vertical integration investments function asprivate equityactivity within the operating company, ensuring continued access to the rare materials and artisanal skills that define Hermes products. The family has not established a formal multi-strategyfamily officeor investment arm comparable to those operated by other European industrial families. This reflects a philosophical choice: the Dumas family views Hermes as a generational asset that outperforms any diversified portfolio, and their governance and estate planning activities focus on maintaining family unity and ownership continuity rather than building an investment empire outside the core business.

name: Tethys Invest Family Office

investment_strategy: The Bettencourt family’s wealth traces to Eugène Schueller, who founded L’Oréal in 1909 and built it into what would become the world’s largest beauty company. The family maintained its controlling position across three generations, with the stake passing from Schueller to his daughter Liliane Bettencourt and subsequently to Françoise Bettencourt Meyers. L’Oréal’s market capitalization, which has exceeded $250 billion, makes the family’s approximate 35% stake worth over $85 billion. The company operates 37 brands across four divisions (consumer products, L’Oréal Luxe, professional products, and dermatological beauty) and generates approximately $45 billion in annual revenue. The Bettencourt family exercises its controlling interest through board representation and the family’s historic position as L’Oréal’s anchor shareholder. A significant structural event occurred in 2023 when Nestlé completed its exit from L’Oréal, ending a shareholder relationship that had lasted since 1974. Nestlé’s departure, facilitated through share buybacks, simplified L’Oréal’s shareholder structure and reinforced the Bettencourt family’s dominant position. Tethys Invest manages diversified investments beyond the L’Oréal stake, though the concentration in L’Oréal means that the family’s overall financial position is highly correlated with the company’s stock performance. The investment office maintains allocations across public equities, fixed income, real estate, and select private investments.
private_markets_approach: Tethys Invest’s private markets activity, while less publicly visible than some family offices of comparable wealth, includes investments in technology, health care, and consumer-related ventures. Thefamily officehas participated inventure capitalinvestments in France and Europe, contributing to the growth of the French technology and startup ecosystem. The family’s real estate holdings include properties in Paris and the south of France, consistent with the family’s deep roots in French business and society. These holdings represent private assets managed alongside the more liquid financial portfolio. The Bettencourt Schueller Foundation, one of the largest philanthropic organizations in Europe, represents a major allocation of family resources toward social impact. The foundation’s focus on scientific research, arts and culture, and social solidarity channels significant capital into grants, fellowships, and institutional support. The foundation’s contribution to the restoration of Notre-Dame Cathedral following the 2019 fire was among the most prominent donations from French business families. Fund managers seeking engagement with Tethys Invest should understand that the family office operates with a degree of privacy unusual even among European family offices. The Bettencourt family has historically maintained a low public profile regarding investment activities outside L’Oréal. Investment relationships are built through established networks within the French business and financial community, and the office favors long-term, relationship-based engagement over transactional fund commitments.

Brin has also directed capital toward scientific research, particularly in the life sciences. The Brin Wojcicki Foundation (established with his former wife Anne Wojcicki, co-founder of 23andMe) has funded Parkinson’s disease research, reflecting Brin’s personal connection to the disease through a genetic predisposition identified via his own DNA testing.
